title: GPU microstate warmup investigation and reproducible runbook
body:
Summary:

This note captures our investigation into short-timescale GPU microstate transitions during benchmark warmup and an actionable runbook to get repeatable plateau throughput. We found that seemingly-identical load runs diverge because of a mix of (A) driver/GPU power/pstate transitions, (B) CUDA kernel autotuning choices that change after initial iterations, and (C) host-level thermal throttling that flips scheduler heuristics. The goal here is a pragmatic harness and checklist to reduce noise and a set of lightweight probes to detect the remaining microstate churn.
body_2:
Why this matters:

- Repeated bench runs should produce stable p50/p95 throughput numbers for SLOs and capacity planning.
- Microstate transitions introduce long-tailed noise and make claimed capacity fragile across regions and instance families.
- Fixes must work without heavy-handed artifacts (no manual PCI resets in CI).

Observed failure modes (examples):

1) Kernel autotune divergence:
- On first few iterations, kernels compile/choose launch configs; later iterations use different shared-memory tiling causing 5-12% throughput jumps.
- Happens more with mixed-precision/quantized kernels when sequence lengths vary in warmup.

2) GPU PSTATE / clock stepping:
- Low-load priming causes GPU to stay in low P-state; then a sudden clock boost causes host-side scheduling jitter.
- Instances with aggressive power management (older cloud SKUs) are worst.

3) NVSwitch / multi-GPU sync stalls:
- Small priming batches create recurring tiny stalls at interconnect sync boundaries that vanish after a full-size wave.

Instrumentation we added:

- microstate-probe.sh (lightweight agent that samples: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=clocks.sm,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu,power.draw --format=csv -l 1)
- kernel-log: capture output of our runtime kernel-selection debug hooks for first N tokens (N default 50)
- host-counters: iostat, mpstat sample at 1s to pick up short spikes
- histo: record per-thread tail latencies from client harness at 10ms granularity

Sample run command (bench harness):

./bench-runner --model redwood-open-7b --seq 512 --clients 64 --rps 1200 --warmup-requests 3200 --steady-requests 12000 --warmup-mode=staggered --seed=42423 --collect-probes=./probes/out

Notes on flags:
- warmup-requests: big enough to let kernel autotune and memory alloc patterns stabilize
- warmup-mode=staggered: random-start client ramp-up (see checklist for why)

Warmup heuristics & checklist (run in order):

1) Preflight host-level health:
- Ensure driver matches runtime pinned version.
- Check /proc/interrupts for runaway IRQs.
- If possible, set MIG or persistence mode where supported: nvidia-smi -pm 1

2) Thermal and power baseline:
- Run a 60s single-GPU synthetic load to set clocks (use simple CUDA microbench that triggers heavy SM utilization). This establishes a baseline P-state.
- Wait 30s for temperatures/power draw to settle.

3) Memory and allocator priming:
- Issue a small sequence of allocation-heavy requests to force static workspace allocations in the runtime (typically 2-4 full-context runs).

4) Kernel autotune priming:
- Execute a tiny number of long-sequence requests (N=3) to trigger any JIT/selector paths; capture kernel-log.

5) Staggered client ramp-up:
- Bring clients up in small groups (e.g., 8 clients every 10s) to avoid synchronized arrival bursts that can flip micro-batching decisions in the runtime.

6) Confirm steady metrics before measurement window:
- Check microstate-probe for stable GPU clocks and utilization for 30s
- Confirm kernel-log shows no further kernel changes for the same op signatures
- If any drift remains, extend warmup window in increments of 50% until stable

Reproducibility experiments we recommend:

- Cross-seed runs: run identical config with 3 different RNG seeds to ensure seed hygiene isn't the driver.
- Short/long warmup ablation: compare warmup-requests of 0/400/1600/6400 to quantify stabilization time.
- Prime-only vs. continuous: run a dedicated priming phase then idle 60s to see whether clocks/pstates drop off and reintroduce noise.

Microstate detection heuristics (alerts the harness):

- ClockJitter: if clocks.sm changes by >5% within the measurement window, flag.
- KernelFlip: if kernel selection table differs between warmup start and end, flag.
- UtilTail: if 95th util / median util > 1.4 for more than 30s, flag.

Quick triage playbook (when a run is noisy):

1) Re-run with microstate-probe enabled and warmup-requests=4x default. If kernelflip disappears, attribute to autotune.
2) Force persistence/power mode and repeat. If noise drops, mark SKU as high-variance and add to SKU blacklist for critical claims.
3) If still noisy, try disabling kernel caching mechanisms in runtime (use DEBUG kernel selector) and re-run to isolate runtime code paths.

Minimal harness changes implemented (notes for infra team):

- new flag --capture-kernel-signature that snapshots kernel hashes for first M invocations
- probe collector service that aggregates per-run microstate CSVs and uploads to S3 with run metadata
- bench-runner now exposes an endpoint /bench/state that returns {run_id, warmup_done, microstate_flags} (JSON only in code; the harness archives as text)

Data formats we store: (example fields)
- run_id, model, instance_type, seed, warmup_requests, clients, capture_start_ts, capture_end_ts, microstate_flags

Best-practice defaults for our CI and lab runs:

- warmup-requests: 3200 for 8xA10 (adjust scale linearly with GPU count)
- warmup-mode: staggered
- capture-probes: enabled for first N runs of a new model or new SKU

Open questions / research items:

- Can we upstream a small GPU micro-burner that triggers stable high-P-state without model-specific allocations? This would make warmup faster and less brittle.
- How do cloud hypervisor live-migration heuristics affect clocks/power over longer runs? Need multi-hour traces.
- Should we fingerprint kernel selection deterministically and store as part of model metadata to detect surprising changes across runtime upgrades?

Appendix: diagnostic snippets and examples:

1) microstate-probe.sh (trimmed)
#!/bin/bash
while true; do
  ts=$(date -Iseconds)
  nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,clocks.sm,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu,power.draw --format=csv,noheader,nounits | awk -v t=\"$ts\" '{print t","$0}'
  sleep 1
done

2) kernel-signature sample (how we hash):
- For each kernel: name + PTX checksum + shared_mem_bytes + block_dim -> md5 -> recorded as kernel_hash

3) example small bench-runner profile capture (excerpt):
run_id: bench-2025-11-15-evm-01
seed: 42423
clients: 64
warmup_requests: 3200
microstate_flags: [ClockJitter]
mean_throughput: 12540 rps
steady_p95_latency_ms: 210
notes: observed kernel_flip at iteration 18; extended warmup to 6400 removed flip

Contact / next steps:
- Owner: Evan Martinez (evan@redwood.ai)
- Follow-up: create automated job that runs priming-only step in CI before any benchmark jobs to establish clocks and kernel-caches
- Action: Add a post-run validator that rejects runs with microstate_flags != [] for commit gating

This doc is intentionally procedural; feel free to copy snippets into a new notebook and iterate.
